awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Social Adaptations and Recovery After Natural Disasters
awd_abstract_narration:
This doctoral dissertation research studies the differential impacts and experiences of repeated natural disasters on different social groups to understand the social variations in adaptation and recovery. The investigators specifically test for the differential impacts of social and economic support, overall health status, and emergency resource management on post disaster outcomes. In addition to providing scientific training for a graduate student in anthropology, broader impacts of the project will inform public disaster management strategies and contribute to the knowledge base that addresses the variations across vulnerable populations facing repeated natural disasters. 

In order to understand the adaptations of different social groups to natural disasters, the investigators utilize qualitative research methods that include semi-structured interviews and behavioral observations in regions with repeated natural disasters. The research expands the anthropological science of adaptations to natural disaster management and makes clear contributions to medical and environmental anthropology, public health, and disability studies. It provides science-based insights that inform the development of sustainable and robust disaster response and recovery strategies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This study contributes insight into the intersection of disability and disaster among marginalized groups living in Eastern North Carolina, a geographic area prone to repeated weather disasters. This study illustrates the complexity of the concepts of disability and disaster by showing how different groups perceive and experience these concepts. This study has important implications for emergency and disaster management. 

Project fieldwork was conducted throughout Eastern North Carolina, primarily taking place in Greenville, North Carolina, from July 2025 to June 2026. During this time, participant observation, in-depth interviews, and weekly check-in phone calls were conducted to explore how disability and disasters are defined and experienced by various participant groups. These groups included disaster and emergency management professionals, disability advocacy professionals, and community members with disabilities and other health conditions.

During the first two months of fieldwork, a sampling frame was defined with the assistance of staff working at a Center for Independent Living and a Healthcare Preparedness Coalition. Participant observation was utilized to better understand the daily operations of each site and the types of communities they serve. Interviews were conducted with staff to explore their own perspectives and opinions on disability and disaster, specifically in Eastern North Carolina. A total of 15 staff members across both research sites were interviewed for this study.

Once the sampling frame was defined, community members were recruited primarily from the Center of Independent Living. As such, 16 people with disabilities were recruited and interviewed for this study. Recruitment of non-disabled community members to form a sample similar to that of disabled community members was difficult in this region. As such, only 2 people without disabilities were recruited and interviewed for this study. A total of 18 community members participated in this study, resulting in a total sample of 33 participants including staff members. The Co-PI conducted a total of 43 interviews and 62 phone calls across all participant groups.

This project reveals that “disaster” does not mean the same thing to everyone. Professionals working in emergency and disaster management view disasters as weather-related events that commonly affect Eastern North Carolina, such as hurricanes, flooding, and winter storms. Professionals working in disability advocacy and people with disabilities (PWDs) themselves view disasters in a broader way. Disasters can be weather-related events, but they can also be personal crises and struggles such as living in poverty, not having access to transportation, and not having accessible or safe housing. This study showed that although PWDs are concerned with weather disasters that might directly impact them, they prioritize their everyday survival over disaster preparedness. PWDs are often left out of traditional disaster planning and policy efforts because their personal crises, or “everyday disasters”, are not recognized as disasters. The primary research findings are:

  • Disaster management professionals operate on clearly defined phases of disaster planning, preparedness, response, and recovery; however, these phases do not account for the everyday conditions and underlying vulnerabilities faced by PWDs
  • Although disaster professionals expressed that disaster preparedness and recovery information was readily available for community members, this information was often not available in accessible, easy to understand formats. Community members did not know where or how to access this information or how to incorporate this information in their daily lives.
  • PWDs cannot prioritize disaster preparedness (specifically for weather disasters) because their personal “everyday disasters” require their full attention and resources. It is not possible to prepare for a winter storm by stocking up on supplies when you have limited to no income. PWDs might be unsure of where their next meal is coming from, let alone a meal they need to have in a week.
  • Disaster management policy and practice, as written, neglects the diversity of underlying conditions faced by PWDs. Disaster response and recovery plans focus on immediate response efforts and distribution of resources for adequate recovery. This ignores the baseline condition PWDs had before disasters occur, creates compounding disaster experiences for PWDs, and leads to chronic cycles of disaster recovery.

This study has relevance to anthropology, public health, disaster studies, and disability studies. It explores what it means to be disabled in an area facing environmental uncertainty while also dealing with everyday personal crises. It contributes to anthropological theory and methods by expanding on ideas of slow violence, slow emergencies, disability expertise, and chronic recovery. This study broadly addresses the issue of sustainable and equitable disaster management, especially during a time where uncertainty is increasing on a global level, and it explores what inclusive emergency management may look like with input from PWDs. Because this project revealed that both disability and disaster are individualized experiences, it contributes to our broader understandings of human ability and experience as well as societal attitudes and beliefs about marginalized groups.
